final.title: Exception queues before automation
final.body:
Before you automate anything, look at the exception queue first. That is the work that falls out of the main workflow: customer questions that need a different answer, invoice mismatches, data corrections, or other cases that interrupt the day. If you cannot name the queue, you usually cannot automate it cleanly either.

The practical test is simple. For one week, track one queue and note three things: how many exceptions arrive, how long each one takes to resolve, and what rule the team uses to decide the outcome. Then ask whether the queue is routine, mixed, or ad-hoc. Routine work is the best candidate for a narrow pilot. Mixed queues still need human review built in. Ad-hoc work often stays manual, because the pattern is not doing much of the heavy lifting.

Keep the control rules visible. If the queue touches approvals, thresholds, audit trails, money movement, or other high-risk decisions, human sign-off stays in place. Automation can organise the review, but it does not replace the person who has to own the decision.

If the data lives in email, spreadsheets, or someone’s head, clean that up before you think about automation. A short, honest inventory of one exception queue is often the right first step. Less glamorous than a model, but harder to argue with.
